title: MSc Economics Starter Kit
text: This document provides resources to prepare for the MSc Economics programme at the University of Leeds. It outlines the prior knowledge assumed in the core modules of the programme. References are given to help you refresh your knowledge and address any gaps before the programme begins. The document also provides a set of multiple choice quizzes to test your knowledge and identify any gaps. Incoming students are strongly encouraged to review the material listed below before commencing their studies.

7.1 Question 1: GDP identity
The GDP identity for an open economy (where \(Y\): GDP, \(C\): consumption, \(G\): government consumption, \(I\): investment, \(M\): imports, \(X\): exports) is:

B. \(Y = C + G + I + M - X\)
C. \(Y = C + G + I + X - M\)
D. \(Y = C + X - M\)

A. \((S - T) + (T - G) = (X - M)\)
B. \((S - I) + (T - G) = (X - M)\)
C. \((S - I) + (T - G) = (M - X)\)
D. \((S - I) + (G - T) = (X - M)\),

8.1 Question 1. Budget Constraints
A consumer faces a price of £5 for Good \(X\) and £10 for Good \(Y\), with an income of £100. If the government imposes a 20% tax on Good \(X\) and gives the consumer a £20 cash transfer, what is the new budget constraint equation?


\(5x + 10y = 120\)


\(6x + 10y = 120\)


\(6x + 12y = 120\)


\(6x + 10y = 100\)

title: MSc Economics Starter Kit
section: 8.2 Question 2. Indifference Curves and Marginal Rate of Substitution (MRS)
text:
8.2 Question 2. Indifference Curves and Marginal Rate of Substitution (MRS)
Why do standard indifference curves typically exhibit a diminishing marginal rate of substitution (\(MRS\))?


Because consumers always prefer extreme bundles to balanced consumption bundles.


Because as a consumer has more of Good \(X\), they are willing to give up increasingly more of Good \(Y\) to get an extra unit of \(X\).


Because of the assumption of non-satiation (more is always better).


Because consumers experience a diminishing marginal utility for a good as they consume more of it.

title: MSc Economics Starter Kit
text:
8.3 Question 3. Utility Maximization
A consumer has the utility function \(U(x, y) = xy\). If the price of \(x\) is \(P_x\), the price of \(y\) is \(P_y\), and income is \(M\), what is the optimal demand function for good \(x\)?


\(x^* = \frac{M}{2P_x}\)


\(x^* = \frac{M}{P_x}\)


\(x^* = \frac{2M}{P_x}\)


\(x^* = \frac{M}{P_x + P_y}\)

text:
8.4 Question 4. Income and Substitution Effects
When the price of a normal good falls, how do the substitution effect (SE) and income effect (IE) operate?


SE increases quantity demanded; IE decreases quantity demanded.


SE decreases quantity demanded; IE increases quantity demanded.


Both SE and IE act to increase the quantity demanded.


Both SE and IE act to decrease the quantity demanded.

The income effect is positive and strictly stronger than the substitution effect.

title: MSc Economics Starter Kit

8.7 Question 7. Intertemporal Choice
An individual lives for two periods, earning an income of \(M_1\) in Period 1 and \(M_2\) in Period 2. They can borrow or save at a market interest rate of \(r\). What is the absolute slope of their intertemporal budget line when Period 2 consumption (\(C_2\)) is plotted on the vertical axis and Period 1 consumption (\(C_1\)) is plotted on the horizontal axis?


\(\frac{1}{1+r}\)


\(1 + r\)


\(r\)


\(\frac{M_2}{M_1}\)

8.8 Question 8. Returns to Scale
A production function is given by \(Q = 2L^{0.6}K^{0.4}\). If both labor (\(L\)) and capital (\(K\)) are doubled, what happens to output (\(Q\))?


Output exactly doubles (Constant Returns to Scale).


Output more than doubles (Increasing Returns to Scale).


Output increases but less than doubles (Decreasing Returns to Scale).

title: MSc Economics Starter Kit
text:
8.9 Question 9. Cost Minimization
A firm minimizes its costs for a target output level when which of the following conditions is met?
(Note: \(MP_L\) and \(MP_K\) represent the Marginal Product of labor and capital, respectively; \(w\) represents the wage rate of labor; and \(r\) represents the rental rate of capital).


\(MP_L = MP_K\)


\(\frac{MP_L}{r} = \frac{MP_K}{w}\)


\(\frac{MP_L}{w} = \frac{MP_K}{r}\)


\(w \cdot L = r \cdot K\)

title: MSc Economics Starter Kit
text:
8.10 Question 10. Profit Maximization
For a perfectly competitive, price-taking firm, why does the general profit-maximizing condition \(MR = MC\) simplify down to \(P = MC\)?


Because the firm can change its price at will to match costs.


Because the firm faces a perfectly elastic demand curve, meaning the market price is constant for any quantity they sell.


Because the firm experiences constant returns to scale at all levels of output.


Because total cost is always equal to total revenue in competition.

title: MSc Economics Starter Kit
text:
8.11 Question 11. Market Equilibria
Suppose a competitive market is initially in long-run equilibrium. If the government introduces a specific per-unit tax paid by consumers, what is the ultimate long-run effect on the price received by producers and the number of firms in the industry, assuming a constant-cost industry?


The price received by producers falls; the number of firms decreases.


The price received by producers remains unchanged; the number of firms decreases.


The price received by producers remains unchanged; the number of firms remains unchanged.


The price received by producers falls; the number of firms remains unchanged.

title: MSc Economics Starter Kit
section: 8.12 Question 12. Corner Solutions and Consumer Optimization
text:
8.12 Question 12. Corner Solutions and Consumer Optimization
Sketch Exercise: On a clean grid, sketch a standard downward-sloping linear budget line. Now, draw a map of downward-sloping linear indifference curves representing perfect substitutes, making your indifference curves strictly steeper than the budget line you drew.
Based on your visual map, if the absolute slope of these indifference curves (\(MRS_{xy}\)) is strictly greater than the absolute slope of the budget line (\(\frac{P_x}{P_y}\)), where must the utility-maximizing allocation mathematically lie?


At an interior tangency bundle containing positive amounts of both goods.


At a corner solution along the vertical axis, consuming exclusively Good Y \((0, M/P_y)\).


At a corner solution along the horizontal axis, consuming exclusively Good X \((M/P_x, 0)\).


The problem has no solution since standard optimization conditions fail.

title: MSc Economics Starter Kit
text:
8.13 Question 13. Production and Isocost Shifts
Sketch Exercise: Sketch a standard, smoothly curved Isoquant representing a fixed target output level. Tangent to this, draw a straight, downward-sloping Isocost line. Now, sketch a second Isocost line that is strictly flatter than your first one.
If a macroeconomic shock causes a firm’s Isocost line (\(\frac{w}{r}\)) to flatten in this manner, how must the firm adjust its input mix along your smooth convex Isoquant to minimize long-run costs?


The wage rate has risen relative to capital, prompting a substitution toward more Capital (\(K\)).


The wage rate has fallen relative to capital, prompting a substitution toward more Labor (\(L\)).


The firm will scale back both capital and labor evenly due to increasing returns.


Input ratios remain entirely fixed because price changes do not change technological constraints.

title: MSc Economics Starter Kit
text:
8.14 Question 14. Non-Convex Preferences
Imagine a consumer whose indifference curves are structurally concave to the origin (bowed outward), while the budget line remains a standard straight downward-sloping constraint intersecting both axes at 10 units. Where must the optimal consumer choice reside?


At the exact interior midpoint, purchasing 5 units of X and 5 units of Y.


At an interior point where the \(MRS\) equals the price ratio.


At an all-or-nothing corner solution on one of the two axes, depending on which boundary sits on a higher curve.


At any coordinate along the budget line, as utility is completely identical across concave bounds.

section: 8.15 Question 15. Risk Preferences and Expected Utility

8.15 Question 15. Risk Preferences and Expected Utility
A consumer has a utility function over wealth given by \(u(w) = \sqrt{w}\). They are offered a gamble where they have a 50% chance of winning £100 and a 50% chance of winning £0. Which of the following statements correctly identifies their risk preference and their expected utility from this gamble?


Risk-neutral; Expected Utility = 5


Risk-averse; Expected Utility = 5


Risk-seeking; Expected Utility = 10


Risk-averse; Expected Utility = 50

title: MSc Economics Starter Kit

Using the same consumer preferences (\(u(w) = \sqrt{w}\)) and gamble from the previous question (50% chance of £100, 50% chance of £0), what is the consumer’s Certainty Equivalent (\(CE\)) for this gamble?


£50


£25


£10


£0

title: MSc Economics Starter Kit
text:
8.17 Question 17. Risk Premium
An individual with initial wealth of £100 faces a 10% chance of losing £64 due to an accident, leaving them with £36. Their utility function is \(u(w) = \ln(w)\). If a perfectly competitive, actuarially fair insurance company offers a policy to fully cover this risk, the premium charged will exactly equal the expected loss. What is the maximum amount this risk-averse individual would theoretically be willing to pay for this full insurance policy?


Exactly £6.40


Less than £6.40


Greater than £6.40


£0, because the risk of loss is too small to insure.

title: MSc Economics Starter Kit
text:
8.18 Question 18. Intertemporal Choice (Borrowing Constraints)
A consumer earns a high income in Period 2 (\(M_2\)) but zero income in Period 1 (\(M_1 = 0\)). They have standard, smoothly curved convex intertemporal preferences and wish to consume a positive amount in both periods. If the credit market breaks down completely and banks refuse to offer any consumption loans, how will this borrowing constraint impact their optimal choice bundle \((C_1, C_2)\)?


They will experience a corner solution where \(C_1 = 0\) and \(C_2 = M_2\).


They will borrow against \(M_2\) at a shadow interest rate, keeping \(C_1 > 0\).


They will consume a balanced bundle where \(C_1 = C_2 = \frac{M_2}{2}\).


They will choose to save a portion of their Period 1 income for the future.

title: MSc Economics Starter Kit

8.19 Question 19. Market Equilibria (Subsidy Incidence)
The government introduces a specific per-unit cash subsidy paid directly to suppliers in a perfectly competitive market. If the price elasticity of demand is highly inelastic (\(|\epsilon_D| \to 0\)) and the price elasticity of supply is highly elastic (\(\epsilon_S \to \infty\)), who captures the economic benefit of this subsidy?


Producers capture the entire benefit via significantly higher profit margins per unit.


Consumers capture the entire benefit via a price drop that matches the full size of the subsidy.


The subsidy benefit is split equally between consumers and producers regardless of elasticities.


Neither party benefits because subsidies always generate deadweight loss that destroys all value.

title: MSc Economics Starter Kit

8.20 Question 20. Market Equilibria (Externalities and Quotas)
A perfectly competitive market generates a negative production externality (e.g., pollution) for every unit of output produced, causing the Social Marginal Cost (\(SMC\)) to sit strictly above the Private Marginal Cost (\(PMC\)). If the government wants to restore allocative efficiency, it can implement an output quota. To achieve the socially optimal equilibrium, where should this quota be set?


At the exact quantity where the market demand curve intersects the Private Marginal Cost (\(PMC\)) curve.


At a quantity of zero, completely banning the production of the good.


At the exact quantity where the market demand curve intersects the Social Marginal Cost (\(SMC\)) curve.


At a level higher than the competitive equilibrium quantity to generate offsetting tax revenues.
